name: Manakamana
tagline: Wish-fulfilling goddess, 10 minutes up by cable car from the highway
meta_description: Manakamana Temple guide: cable car from Kurintar, darshan timings, fares for Indians, the old pilgrim trail, crowds and how to visit from Pokhara.
summary: Manakamana is one of Nepal's most visited Hindu temples, dedicated to the goddess Bhagwati who is believed to grant wishes. It stands at about 1,300 m on a ridge in Gorkha district, reached by a 2.8 km cable car from Kurintar on the Kathmandu–Pokhara highway. Allow 3–4 hours for darshan, longer on Saturdays.
intro: The name means 'heart's wish', and pilgrims climb to Manakamana to ask the goddess for children, health, success in exams, a good marriage or a new business, returning to give thanks when the wish is granted. The temple is a multi-tiered pagoda in a stone-paved square on top of Kafakdada hill, surrounded by small hotels, puja shops and tea houses. Its priests are, by tradition, descendants of Lakhan Thapa, a Magar devotee linked to the 17th century queen of Gorkha's King Ram Shah, who is said to have been the goddess incarnate.

Until 1998 the only way up was a 3–4 hour climb from Abu Khaireni on the highway. That year Nepal's first commercial cable car opened, a 2,772 m Austrian-built gondola rising from Kurintar at about 258 m to the temple ridge in roughly 10 minutes. Visitor numbers multiplied, and Manakamana is now an easy stop on any road journey between Kathmandu, Pokhara and Chitwan. The ride itself, with the valley dropping away below the cabin, is now part of the pilgrimage.

For Indian pilgrims, Manakamana is often paired with Pashupatinath in Kathmandu and the Gorkha Kalika and Muktinath shrines further west. Animal sacrifice is part of worship here: goats and pigeons are offered in a pavilion behind the temple, especially on Saturdays and during Dashain. Vegetarian and Vaishnav pilgrims can offer flowers, coconuts and sweets at the main shrine and avoid that area entirely. The temple is open every day of the year, with the heaviest crowds on Saturdays, public holidays and during Dashain.
facts: ≈ 105 km · 3.5–4 h to Kurintar + 10 min cable car
Wish-fulfilling Bhagwati temple, Nepal's first passenger cable car

highlights.title: Cable car from Kurintar
highlights.text: The gondola climbs about 1,040 m over 2.8 km in roughly 10 minutes, crossing the Trishuli river valley and terraced hills. Six-seat cabins leave every few minutes. Look back for the river and forward for the temple ridge; on clear days the Himalaya appears as you near the top.

highlights.title: Darshan of Manakamana Bhagwati
highlights.text: Queue in the stone square to enter the shrine, offer flowers, red powder, coconut and sweets, and ring the temple bells as you leave. On weekdays the queue is often 20–40 minutes; on Saturdays and festival days it can run to several hours.

highlights.title: Himalayan view from the ridge
highlights.text: From the top of Kafakdada the northern skyline shows Manaslu, Himalchuli and Baudha Himal, with the Annapurnas further west on clear mornings. A short walk behind the temple to the viewpoint gives the open panorama without the crowd.

highlights.title: The old pilgrim trail
highlights.text: Before the cable car, pilgrims walked up from Abu Khaireni or Anbu Khaireni on the Prithvi Highway, a climb of about 3–4 hours through villages and forest. The trail is still used and makes a satisfying half-day hike for fit walkers.

highlights.title: Temple square and bazaar
highlights.text: Lanes around the temple sell puja baskets, bangles, red threads, sindoor, brass lamps and local sweets. Simple restaurants serve dal bhat and vegetarian thalis, and several small hotels allow pilgrims to stay overnight for the morning aarti.

highlights.title: Combine with Gorkha
highlights.text: Gorkha's hilltop palace and Kalika temple are about 50 km away by road via Abu Khaireni. Many pilgrims do Manakamana in the morning and Gorkha the same afternoon or the next day, making a two-shrine darshan between Kathmandu and Pokhara.

how_to_reach.text: Kurintar, the cable car base, is on the Prithvi Highway about 105 km from Kathmandu (3.5–4 h), about 115 km from Pokhara (3.5–4 h) and about 60 km from Chitwan's Sauraha (1.5–2 h) via Mugling. There is a large car park at the station. Tourist buses between Kathmandu and Pokhara or Chitwan will drop you at Kurintar on request.

The traditional trail starts at Abu Khaireni on the highway west of Mugling and climbs about 1,000 m to the temple in 3–4 hours. Carry water and start early to avoid the midday heat. Many walkers hike up and take the cable car down.

where_to_stay: Most visitors do Manakamana as a stop on the road between Kathmandu and Pokhara and sleep in Pokhara, Bandipur or Gorkha the same night. On the ridge there are a number of small, basic hotels and pilgrim lodges around the temple square, with simple rooms and vegetarian meals, useful if you want to attend the early morning aarti before the first cable cars arrive. Down at Kurintar there are a few riverside resorts along the Trishuli on the highway. For a comfortable night with character, we usually continue to The Old Inn in Bandipur, about 1.5 hours west.
tips: Avoid Saturdays and Dashain if you dislike crowds; queues for the cable car and the shrine can exceed two to three hours.
Reach Kurintar when the cable car opens in the morning to beat the tour buses from Kathmandu and Pokhara.
Pilgrims who prefer not to see animal sacrifice should avoid the pavilion behind the temple, especially on Saturdays.
Leather items are not allowed inside the shrine, so leave belts and bags with your driver or at a shop.
Carry Nepali rupees for the cable car ticket and offerings; Indian adults pay a separate rupee fare.

experiences.title: Manakamana cable car and temple darshan
experiences.summary: Ride Nepal's first passenger cable car 2.8 km up from Kurintar to the Manakamana temple ridge, queue for darshan of the wish-fulfilling goddess and take in the Himalayan view before riding down. The standard stop on Kathmandu–Pokhara road journeys.
body: The cable car station at Kurintar sits beside the Prithvi Highway with a large car park, ticket counters and a waiting hall. Fares are charged by nationality, with separate rates for Nepali citizens, Indian citizens, other SAARC visitors and other foreigners, and child fares by height. Six-seat cabins leave every few minutes and climb about 1,040 m in roughly 10 minutes, passing over the Trishuli valley, terraced fields and forest. Separate cargo cabins carry goats for sacrifice, which surprises many first-time visitors.

From the top station it is a five-minute walk past puja shops to the temple square. Buy a puja basket of flowers, red powder, coconut, incense and sweets, and join the queue. Inside, the goddess is represented by a stone image; priests accept offerings, mark your forehead with tika and return prasad. Walk around the temple clockwise, ring the bells and tie a red thread or offer a lamp if you are making a wish.

After darshan, walk five minutes to the viewpoint behind the temple for the mountains, then have tea or a vegetarian lunch in the bazaar. Allow about three hours in total on a weekday. On Saturdays and festival days, especially Dashain in October, queues for the cable car and the shrine can take three hours or more. Operating hours change by season and include a midday break, so check current timings before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the Manakamana cable car fare for Indians?
faqs.a: Indian citizens pay a separate rupee fare, which has been around NPR 880 return for adults with a lower child fare, while other foreigners pay about US$ 20 return and Nepali citizens less. Children are charged by height. Fares are revised from time to time, so check the current tariff at Kurintar or on the operator's site before you travel.

faqs.q: How long is the queue at Manakamana?
faqs.a: On weekday mornings outside festivals, expect 15–30 minutes for the cable car and 20–40 minutes for the shrine. On Saturdays, public holidays and during Dashain, each queue can take two to three hours or more. Arrive when the cable car opens and avoid Saturdays to keep the visit to about three hours.

faqs.q: Is the Manakamana cable car safe for elderly pilgrims?
faqs.a: Yes. The cabins are enclosed, seated and step-free to board with staff assistance, and the ride is smooth and about 10 minutes long. At the top there is a short walk on paved lanes with some steps to the temple. Elderly pilgrims should avoid Saturday crowds, which involve long standing queues in the sun.

experiences.title: Hike the old pilgrim trail to Manakamana
experiences.summary: Walk up to Manakamana the way pilgrims did for three centuries before the cable car: a climb of about 1,000 m from Abu Khaireni on the Prithvi Highway through villages, terraces and forest, then ride the cable car down to Kurintar.
body: The trail begins near Abu Khaireni, on the Prithvi Highway between Dumre and Mugling, where the Marsyangdi river runs below the road. A stone path climbs steadily up the hillside towards the temple ridge through small Gurung, Magar and Brahmin settlements, rice and millet terraces and patches of sal and chilaune forest. Tea shops along the way still serve walkers, though far fewer than before 1998. The route was the main approach for pilgrims for about three centuries.

Expect 3–4 hours of uphill walking with about 1,000 m of height gain, grade moderate. The trail is clear and well used by local people, but a guide helps at junctions and explains the villages and shrines you pass. As you climb, the views open over the Marsyangdi and Trishuli valleys and, near the top, north to Manaslu and Himalchuli on clear mornings. Expect to meet villagers carrying loads and the occasional pilgrim who still prefers to walk for religious reasons.

Arriving on foot, you enter the temple square from the back, the way the old pilgrims did. After darshan and lunch, ride the cable car down to Kurintar, where your vehicle can be waiting. Start by 7 am to avoid walking in the midday heat, carry 2 litres of water and avoid the monsoon months, when the trail is slippery and leeches appear in the forest sections. Total walking time is about 3–4 hours.

faqs.q: How long does it take to walk up to Manakamana?
faqs.a: About 3–4 hours from Abu Khaireni for a reasonably fit walker, gaining roughly 1,000 m. Coming down on foot takes about 2–3 hours, though most people take the cable car down to Kurintar. Start early in the morning, especially from March onwards when midday temperatures in the valley reach 30 °C.

faqs.q: Is the Manakamana walking trail safe?
faqs.a: Yes. It is a busy local path through villages, used daily by residents and some pilgrims, and the main risks are heat, dehydration and slippery steps in rain. Walk with a companion or guide, carry water and snacks, and avoid the trail during heavy monsoon rain from July to August.

faqs.q: Can I walk up and take the cable car down?
faqs.a: Yes, and this is the most popular way to combine the two. Buy a one-way downhill ticket at the top station. Arrange for your car to wait at Kurintar, which is a different point on the highway from the Abu Khaireni trailhead, about 20–30 minutes apart by road.

experiences.title: Sunrise on the Manakamana ridge
experiences.summary: Stay a night in a pilgrim lodge on the ridge and you have Manakamana almost to yourself at dawn: morning aarti at the temple, then sunrise on Manaslu, Himalchuli and the Annapurnas from the viewpoint behind the square, before the first cable car arrives.
body: Few foreign visitors stay overnight at Manakamana, which is exactly why it is worth considering. When the last cable car goes down in the late afternoon, the temple square empties and the ridge becomes a quiet village again. Small lodges around the square offer simple rooms and vegetarian dal bhat. In the evening, lamps are lit at the shrine and local families gather for prayers. It is a very different atmosphere from the busy daytime temple.

Wake before dawn for the morning worship at the temple, when the queue is short and the atmosphere unhurried. Then walk a few minutes to the viewpoint behind the temple. From October to February, the sky usually clears at first light to show Manaslu (8,163 m), Himalchuli and Baudha Himal to the north, with the Annapurna range to the north-west, while the valleys of the Trishuli and Marsyangdi lie in cloud below.

By 9 am the first cable cars bring the day's pilgrims and the square fills again. Have breakfast, then ride down to Kurintar to continue to Gorkha, Bandipur, Pokhara or Chitwan. Lodges on the ridge are basic, with shared or simple attached bathrooms, so this suits pilgrims and travellers who value the experience over comfort. Bring a torch, a warm layer for the early morning and cash for the lodge, since cards are rarely accepted. Rooms around the square fill on Friday nights before the Saturday crowds, so book ahead if your visit falls then.

faqs.q: Can you stay overnight at Manakamana temple?
faqs.a: Yes. A number of small hotels and pilgrim lodges stand around the temple square, offering simple rooms and vegetarian meals. Standards are basic. Staying lets you attend the quiet morning worship and see sunrise before the cable car brings the crowds. Book ahead for Saturdays and the Dashain festival period.

faqs.q: Which mountains can you see from Manakamana?
faqs.a: On a clear morning from October to February you see Manaslu (8,163 m), Himalchuli and Baudha Himal directly north, with the Annapurna range and sometimes Lamjung Himal further west. Views are best at sunrise and usually cloud over by late morning. From June to September the peaks are rarely visible.

Restaurants around the temple serve mainly vegetarian food, including dal bhat, puri tarkari and sweets, though some also serve meat outside the temple area because animal sacrifice is part of local worship. Pilgrims who want strictly vegetarian or Jain meals should ask, or eat at their hotel.

faqs.q: What is the history of Manakamana Temple?
faqs.a: Tradition links the temple to the queen of King Ram Shah of Gorkha in the 17th century, believed to be an incarnation of the goddess, and to her devotee Lakhan Thapa, a Magar whose descendants still serve as the temple's priests. The present pagoda has been rebuilt and repaired several times, most recently after the 2015 earthquake.

faqs.q: What are the Manakamana cable car timings?
faqs.a: The cable car generally runs from about 9 am to 5 pm, with an earlier start on Saturdays and festival days and a short break around lunchtime. Timings change by season and on special days. Check current status before you travel, and aim to arrive early in the day to avoid long queues.

faqs.q: How far is Manakamana from Pokhara?
faqs.a: Kurintar, the cable car base, is about 115 km east of Pokhara on the Prithvi Highway, a drive of 3.5–4 hours via Damauli and Mugling. Add 10 minutes for the cable car. Many travellers visit on the road between Pokhara and Kathmandu or between Pokhara and Chitwan.

faqs.q: Is Manakamana on the way from Kathmandu to Pokhara?
faqs.a: Yes. Kurintar is on the Prithvi Highway about 105 km from Kathmandu, roughly halfway to Pokhara. A darshan stop adds 3–4 hours to the journey on a normal weekday, so a full day of 10–11 hours from Kathmandu to Pokhara. Breaking the journey at Bandipur makes it more comfortable.

faqs.q: Why are animals sacrificed at Manakamana?
faqs.a: Many devotees offer a goat or pigeon to the goddess Bhagwati in thanks for a wish fulfilled, a practice common at Shakti temples in Nepal. Sacrifices take place in a pavilion behind the main temple, mostly on Saturdays and during Dashain. Pilgrims can worship with flowers, coconut and sweets and avoid the area.

faqs.q: Can children and seniors visit Manakamana?
faqs.a: Yes. The cable car makes the temple accessible to almost everyone, with enclosed seated cabins and a short walk at the top. Children below a set height ride at a lower fare. The main difficulty is long queues in sun on busy days, so visit on a weekday morning and carry water and caps.

faqs.q: What should I wear to Manakamana Temple?
faqs.a: Modest clothing covering shoulders and knees. Remove shoes before entering the shrine area; shoe stands are provided. Leather belts and bags are not allowed inside the temple. In winter mornings bring a light jacket for the ridge, and in summer a cap and sunscreen for queues.

faqs.q: Is Manakamana open during the monsoon?
faqs.a: Yes, the temple is open all year and the cable car runs in the monsoon except during storms, power issues or maintenance. Rain and cloud hide the mountain views from June to September, and the highway to Kurintar can be slowed by landslides. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I visit Manakamana and Gorkha in one day?
faqs.a: Yes, by car. Do Manakamana when the cable car opens, drive about 50 km to Gorkha via Abu Khaireni (1.5–2 h), and climb to Gorkha Durbar and the Kalika temple in the afternoon. You can sleep in Gorkha, or drive on to Pokhara, 3–3.5 hours away, arriving in the evening.
